fields.definition: A large-format modular synthesizer standard whose module front panels are five rack units tall (about 8.75 in / 222 mm), typically patched with 1/4-inch (6.35 mm) cables and following the 1 volt-per-octave control standard. It is the format of classic Moog modular systems and modern lines such as Synthesizers.com (Dotcom), MOTM, and Moog Unit (MU) modulars.
fields.plain_english: A large style of modular synth. Each part has a tall panel, about 8.75 inches high. The big size leaves room for large knobs and thick 1/4-inch cables, like classic studio gear from the 1960s and 70s.
fields.purpose_function: The tall panels give room for full-size knobs, switches, and widely spaced jacks, making complex patches easy to see and adjust, while the format preserves the look and workflow of classic 1960s-70s modular systems.
fields.practical_application: A technician builds or maintains 5U systems by matching panel formats and connection conventions (1/4-inch jacks, and S-trig versus V-trig gates on vintage Moog gear) so modules from different makers interconnect correctly.
common_mistakes: Treating '5U' as a single interchangeable standard, when MU (Moog), Dotcom, and MOTM differ in jacks, triggers, and power headers.
Expecting vintage Moog S-trig gates to drive modern V-trig inputs without a converter.
Reversing a module's power connector; verify pin-out and polarity before applying power to avoid damaging the module.
scenario_contexts: Restoring a vintage Moog modular and matching replacement modules to the original 5U panel and trigger format.
Building a new large-format studio synth from Synthesizers.com Dotcom modules with a matched power supply.
Interfacing a 5U system with a Eurorack case using a format-bridging or level-shifting adapter.

sources: Mark Vail, The Synthesizer (Oxford University Press)

fields.definition: A modular-synthesizer format introduced by Doepfer (A-100 series, mid-1990s) in which module panels are 3U (128.5 mm) tall and their width is measured in horizontal pitch (HP, where 1 HP = 5.08 mm). Modules are patched with 3.5 mm (1/8-inch) cables, follow the 1 volt-per-octave pitch standard, and draw power over a ribbon connector supplying plus/minus 12 V (and often +5 V).
fields.plain_english: A popular small format for modular synths. Each part is about 5 inches tall and uses thin 1/8-inch cables. Because the parts are small, you can fit many of them in one case.
fields.purpose_function: Its small module size and shared power and signal standards let a technician fit many modules from many makers into one case, which has made Eurorack the most widely used modular format today.
fields.practical_application: Technicians assemble Eurorack systems by budgeting HP width and power-rail current, aligning the ribbon cable's red stripe to the -12 V pins, and patching CV, gate, and audio between modules with 3.5 mm cables.
common_mistakes: Reversing the power ribbon: the red stripe must align with -12 V on both the module header and the bus board, or the module can be damaged.
Overloading a power rail by adding modules without totaling each rail's current draw against the supply's rating.
Confusing HP (panel width) with U (panel height) when planning a build.
Assuming Eurorack CV/gate levels and 3.5 mm cables interconnect directly with 5U systems.
scenario_contexts: Planning a case build by summing +12 V and -12 V current draw for every module before choosing a power supply.
Troubleshooting a dead module after a ribbon cable was plugged in upside down.
Patching an external CV keyboard into a Eurorack oscillator's 1V/octave input.

sources: Mark Vail, The Synthesizer (Oxford University Press)

fields.definition: In modular and CV systems, a trigger is a brief voltage pulse that signals the instant an event should begin, such as starting an envelope, advancing a sequencer step, or firing a drum voice. Unlike a gate, which stays high for the full duration of a note, a trigger conveys only the moment of onset, not how long to hold.
fields.plain_english: A trigger is a quick pulse of voltage that tells a module to start something, like firing a drum or an envelope. Think of it as a tap on the shoulder: it marks the moment to go, but not how long to hold.
fields.purpose_function: A trigger tells modules exactly when to act, keeping envelopes, sequencers, and drum modules synced to a rhythmic event without carrying any duration information.
fields.practical_application: A technician routes a trigger from a clock, sequencer, or drum pad to a module's trigger input to fire it, and must match the trigger type (positive-going V-trig versus switch-to-ground S-trig on some vintage gear), using a converter when they differ.
common_mistakes: Confusing a trigger with a gate: a trigger marks only the onset, while a gate also holds the note and controls sustain and release.
Expecting a trigger alone to sustain an ADSR envelope, when the sustain stage needs a held gate.
Mixing S-trig (switch/short-to-ground, e.g. vintage Moog) and V-trig (positive voltage) signals without a converter, so nothing fires.
Assuming all triggers share one voltage, when some modules need a minimum level (often around +2 to +5 V) to register.
scenario_contexts: Clocking a drum module by sending a trigger pulse to each voice's trigger input.
Advancing an analog sequencer one step per incoming trigger.
Adapting a vintage Moog S-trig keyboard to fire a modern V-trig envelope through a converter.

sources: Curtis Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press)
Mark Vail, The Synthesizer (Oxford University Press)
